subject: Chemistry
question: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon in which a substance accumulates
options: at the surface of another substance
uniformly throughout the bulk of another substance
only at the centre of a solid
only in the gaseous state
explanation: Adsorption refers to the accumulation of molecules of a substance (adsorbate) specifically at the surface of another substance (adsorbent), rather than being distributed uniformly throughout its bulk

subject: Chemistry
question: Absorption differs from adsorption in that absorption involves the substance being
options: uniformly distributed throughout the bulk of the other substance
confined only to the surface
present only in trace amounts
limited exclusively to gases
explanation: Unlike adsorption, which is a surface phenomenon, absorption involves the substance being taken up and uniformly distributed throughout the entire bulk (volume) of the absorbing material, such as water being absorbed throughout a sponge

subject: Chemistry
question: Adsorption caused by weak van der Waals forces of attraction between adsorbate and adsorbent is called
options: physisorption (physical adsorption)
chemisorption (chemical adsorption)
absorption
diffusion
explanation: Physisorption, or physical adsorption, occurs when the adsorbate molecules are held to the adsorbent surface by relatively weak van der Waals forces of attraction

subject: Chemistry
question: Adsorption involving the formation of strong chemical bonds between adsorbate and adsorbent is called
options: chemisorption (chemical adsorption)
physisorption (physical adsorption)
absorption
dialysis
explanation: Chemisorption, or chemical adsorption, occurs when adsorbate molecules are held to the surface of the adsorbent through the formation of strong chemical bonds, similar in strength to ordinary chemical bond formation

subject: Chemistry
question: Physisorption is generally characterized by
options: low enthalpy of adsorption and reversibility
very high enthalpy of adsorption and irreversibility
the formation of a chemical compound
occurring only at very high temperatures
explanation: Physisorption is characterized by a relatively low enthalpy of adsorption (typically 20-40 kJ/mol) due to weak van der Waals interactions, and is generally readily reversible, since increasing the temperature can easily desorb the physisorbed molecules

subject: Chemistry
question: Chemisorption is generally characterized by
options: high enthalpy of adsorption and irreversibility
very low enthalpy of adsorption and easy reversibility
occurring only in the gaseous state with no solid surface required
the complete absence of any activation energy
explanation: Chemisorption is characterized by a comparatively high enthalpy of adsorption (typically 80-240 kJ/mol) due to the formation of strong chemical bonds, and is generally irreversible under ordinary conditions, since breaking these chemical bonds requires considerable energy

subject: Chemistry
question: Physisorption generally decreases with an increase in temperature because
options: higher thermal energy overcomes the weak van der Waals forces holding the adsorbate to the surface
higher temperature strengthens the intermolecular forces of attraction
chemisorption always increases whenever physisorption decreases
temperature has no effect whatsoever on any type of adsorption
explanation: Since physisorption relies on relatively weak van der Waals forces, increasing the temperature provides sufficient thermal energy to overcome these weak attractive forces, causing the adsorbed molecules to desorb and physisorption to decrease

subject: Chemistry
question: An adsorption isotherm is a graph that shows the variation of the amount of gas adsorbed on a solid surface with
options: pressure of the gas at a constant temperature
temperature at a constant pressure
time at a constant pressure and temperature
the surface area of the adsorbent alone
explanation: An adsorption isotherm is a graphical representation showing how the amount of gas adsorbed on a solid surface varies with the equilibrium pressure of the gas, measured at a constant, fixed temperature

subject: Chemistry
question: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm is expressed mathematically as ˣ⁄ₘ = k × p raised to the power
options: ¹⁄ₙ, where n is a constant greater than 1
n, where n equals exactly 1 in all cases
-¹⁄ₙ exclusively
2n, with no other possible values of the exponent
explanation: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm is expressed as ˣ⁄ₘ=k p^(¹⁄ₙ), where ˣ⁄ₘ represents the mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent, p is the equilibrium pressure, and k and n are empirical constants that depend on the nature of the adsorbate and adsorbent

subject: Chemistry
question: Activated charcoal is commonly used in gas masks primarily because of its ability to
options: adsorb toxic gases onto its extensive surface area
chemically react with and destroy all toxic gases permanently
absorb gases uniformly throughout its bulk structure
repel all gases without any interaction
explanation: Activated charcoal, having an extremely large and porous surface area, is highly effective at adsorbing toxic gases and vapors onto its surface, making it a key component in gas masks and various filtration and purification applications

subject: Chemistry
question: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without
options: itself undergoing any permanent chemical change
participating in the reaction in any way whatsoever
affecting the rate of the reaction at all
being present in the reaction mixture
explanation: A catalyst is defined as a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change by the end of the reaction

subject: Chemistry
question: A promoter is a substance that, when added in small quantities along with a catalyst, serves to
options: increase the catalytic activity or efficiency of the catalyst
decrease the catalytic activity of the catalyst
replace the catalyst entirely in the reaction
act as the primary reactant in the overall reaction
explanation: A promoter is a substance added in small amounts along with a catalyst that enhances or increases the catalytic activity and efficiency of the primary catalyst, without itself possessing significant catalytic activity on its own

subject: Chemistry
question: A catalytic poison is a substance that, when present even in small amounts, tends to
options: decrease or completely destroy the activity of a catalyst
increase the activity of a catalyst significantly
have no effect whatsoever on catalytic activity
act as an additional catalyst alongside the original one
explanation: A catalytic poison is a substance that, often by strongly adsorbing onto and blocking the active sites of a catalyst, decreases or entirely destroys the catalytic activity of the catalyst, reducing or stopping the reaction it was facilitating

subject: Chemistry
question: Homogeneous catalysis occurs when the catalyst and the reactants exist in the
options: same phase
different phases from one another
gaseous state exclusively regardless of the reactants' phase
solid state exclusively regardless of the reactants' phase
explanation: Homogeneous catalysis is defined as catalysis in which the catalyst and all the reactants exist together in the same physical phase, such as all being present in a single liquid solution

subject: Chemistry
question: Heterogeneous catalysis occurs when the catalyst and the reactants exist in
options: different phases from one another
the exact same single phase
the gaseous phase only for both catalyst and reactants
no phase at all, being entirely theoretical
explanation: Heterogeneous catalysis is defined as catalysis in which the catalyst exists in a different physical phase from the reactants, most commonly involving a solid catalyst facilitating the reaction of gaseous or liquid phase reactants at its surface

subject: Chemistry
question: Autocatalysis refers to a phenomenon in which
options: one of the products formed during a reaction itself acts as a catalyst for that same reaction
the reactants act as catalysts for an entirely unrelated, separate reaction
a reaction proceeds without any catalyst present at any stage
the reaction rate remains completely constant throughout its entire course
explanation: Autocatalysis occurs when one of the products generated during the course of a chemical reaction itself functions as a catalyst for that very same reaction, often resulting in the reaction rate initially increasing as the autocatalytic product accumulates

subject: Chemistry
question: Enzymes are best described as
options: biological catalysts, typically proteins, that increase the rate of specific biochemical reactions
inorganic catalysts used exclusively in industrial processes
substances that always decrease the rate of biochemical reactions
non-specific catalysts that work equally well on virtually any reaction
explanation: Enzymes are highly specific biological catalysts, almost always proteins in nature, that dramatically increase the rate of particular biochemical reactions occurring within living organisms

subject: Chemistry
question: A colloidal system in which the dispersed phase is a solid and the dispersion medium is a liquid is called a
options: sol
gel
foam
aerosol
explanation: A colloidal system with a solid dispersed phase distributed within a liquid dispersion medium is classified as a sol, such as a colloidal solution of gold particles in water

subject: Chemistry
question: A colloidal system in which the dispersed phase is a gas and the dispersion medium is a liquid is called a
options: foam
sol
gel
aerosol
explanation: A colloidal system with a gas dispersed within a liquid dispersion medium is classified as a foam, such as whipped cream or soap lather

subject: Chemistry
question: Colloidal sols in which the dispersed phase particles have a strong affinity or attraction for the dispersion medium are called
options: lyophilic (solvent-loving) sols
lyophobic (solvent-hating) sols
emulsions exclusively
suspensions
explanation: Lyophilic sols are colloidal systems in which the dispersed phase particles have a strong natural affinity for the dispersion medium, and as a result these sols tend to form spontaneously and are generally quite stable

subject: Chemistry
question: Colloidal sols in which the dispersed phase particles have little or no affinity for the dispersion medium are called
options: lyophobic (solvent-hating) sols
lyophilic (solvent-loving) sols
true solutions
gels exclusively
explanation: Lyophobic sols are colloidal systems in which the dispersed phase particles have little to no natural affinity for the dispersion medium, and as a result these sols do not form spontaneously and tend to be comparatively less stable, requiring special preparation methods and stabilizing agents

subject: Chemistry
question: Multimolecular colloids are formed when a large number of small atoms or molecules of a substance
options: aggregate together to form particles within the colloidal size range
dissociate completely into individual, separate ions
react chemically to form an entirely new single large molecule
remain dispersed as individual atoms with no aggregation whatsoever
explanation: Multimolecular colloids form when numerous small atoms or molecules of a substance aggregate or associate together through weak intermolecular forces to form larger particles that fall within the characteristic size range of a colloidal system, such as a sol of gold atoms

subject: Chemistry
question: Macromolecular colloids are formed by substances that naturally exist as
options: large, giant molecules such as proteins or synthetic polymers
exclusively simple, small ionic compounds
gases at ordinary temperature and pressure
only naturally occurring gemstones
explanation: Macromolecular colloids consist of substances that inherently exist as very large (giant) molecules, such as proteins, cellulose, and various synthetic polymers, and these large molecules themselves fall within the colloidal particle size range

subject: Chemistry
question: Associated colloids, such as those formed by soap molecules in water above a certain concentration, are also known as
options: micelles
suspensions
true solutions
emulsions exclusively
explanation: Associated colloids, formed when surfactant molecules like soap aggregate together above a specific critical concentration to form colloidal-sized clusters, are commonly referred to as micelles

subject: Chemistry
question: The Tyndall effect refers to the phenomenon in which colloidal particles
options: scatter a beam of light passed through the colloidal solution, making the path of light visible
completely absorb all light passed through the colloidal solution
allow light to pass through without any scattering or interaction whatsoever
emit their own light spontaneously with no external light source needed
explanation: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles when a beam of light is passed through a colloidal solution, making the path of the light beam visible when viewed from the side, a phenomenon not observed in true solutions

subject: Chemistry
question: Brownian movement refers to the continuous, random, zig-zag motion of colloidal particles caused by
options: continuous, random collisions with the molecules of the dispersion medium
a deliberate external force applied to the colloidal system
gravity acting uniformly on all colloidal particles
the particles chemically reacting with one another continuously
explanation: Brownian movement is the constant, random, zig-zag motion exhibited by colloidal particles, resulting from continuous, random collisions between the dispersed colloidal particles and the rapidly moving molecules of the surrounding dispersion medium

subject: Chemistry
question: Colloidal particles in a given sol typically carry
options: a similar (same sign) electric charge on all particles, contributing to the overall stability of the sol
no electric charge whatsoever under any circumstances
a mixture of both positive and negative charges randomly distributed among particles
a charge that changes randomly and unpredictably at every instant
explanation: Colloidal particles within a given sol typically carry a similar electric charge (either all positive or all negative), and this common charge causes mutual repulsion between particles, which helps prevent them from aggregating together and contributes significantly to the overall stability of the colloidal sol

subject: Chemistry
question: Electrophoresis refers to the movement of charged colloidal particles under the influence of
options: an applied electric field
gravitational force alone
a magnetic field exclusively
increased temperature alone
explanation: Electrophoresis is the phenomenon in which charged colloidal particles migrate towards the oppositely charged electrode when an external electric field is applied across the colloidal solution

subject: Chemistry
question: Coagulation of a colloidal sol refers to the process by which colloidal particles
options: aggregate together and settle out of the dispersion medium as a precipitate
become more finely and uniformly dispersed throughout the medium
completely dissolve into a true solution
evaporate entirely from the dispersion medium
explanation: Coagulation (or precipitation) is the process by which the dispersed colloidal particles aggregate together into larger clusters that eventually settle out of the dispersion medium, often triggered by the addition of an electrolyte that neutralizes the stabilizing charge on the particles

subject: Chemistry
question: An emulsion is a colloidal system formed by the dispersion of one liquid within
options: another immiscible liquid
a solid dispersion medium exclusively
a gaseous dispersion medium exclusively
itself, with no second distinct phase involved
explanation: An emulsion is a colloidal system consisting of small droplets of one liquid dispersed throughout another liquid with which it is normally immiscible, such as oil dispersed in water or water dispersed in oil

subject: Chemistry
question: During the adsorption of a gas on a solid surface, the process is always accompanied by a decrease in entropy because
options: the randomness of gas molecules decreases significantly as they become confined and more ordered upon the solid surface compared to their free movement in the gas phase
the entropy of the solid adsorbent itself increases dramatically to compensate
adsorption always increases the total entropy of the entire system with no exception
entropy changes are entirely irrelevant to the thermodynamics of any adsorption process
explanation: When gas molecules, which possess considerable translational and rotational freedom (high entropy) in the gas phase, become adsorbed onto a solid surface, their movement becomes considerably more restricted and ordered, resulting in a decrease in the entropy of the adsorbed system compared to the free gas phase, which is a general characteristic feature of the adsorption process

subject: Chemistry
question: Despite adsorption typically involving a decrease in entropy (an unfavorable factor for spontaneity), the process remains spontaneous under suitable conditions because
options: adsorption is an exothermic process, releasing enough heat energy such that the accompanying decrease in enthalpy still results in an overall negative (favorable) Gibbs energy change
adsorption is always endothermic with no net enthalpy contribution to consider
entropy changes have no bearing whatsoever on whether adsorption proceeds spontaneously
the temperature during adsorption always increases sufficiently to reverse the sign of the entropy change
explanation: Adsorption is generally an exothermic process (negative δH), and according to the Gibbs energy relation δG=δH - T δS, even though the entropy change (δS) is negative (unfavorable) during adsorption, a sufficiently large negative enthalpy change can still result in an overall negative (favorable, spontaneous) Gibbs energy change, particularly at lower temperatures where the T δS term contributes less unfavorably to the overall equation

subject: Chemistry
question: Unlike physisorption, which occurs to some extent on almost any solid surface for almost any gas, chemisorption is highly specific because
options: chemisorption requires the formation of chemical bonds, which can only occur between specific adsorbate-adsorbent combinations capable of appropriate chemical interaction
physisorption requires much stronger and more specific interactions than chemisorption in every case
chemisorption occurs equally well between literally any pair of adsorbate and adsorbent, with no specificity whatsoever
specificity is a concept that applies only to enzyme catalysis and never to any form of surface adsorption
explanation: Since chemisorption involves the formation of genuine chemical bonds between the adsorbate and specific atoms on the adsorbent surface, it is inherently more selective and specific, occurring only between adsorbate-adsorbent combinations capable of the necessary chemical interaction, unlike physisorption, which relies on more universal, non-specific van der Waals forces that operate to some degree between almost any pair of substances

subject: Chemistry
topic: Adsorption Isotherm: Effect of Pressure at Different Regions
question: In the Freundlich adsorption isotherm plot of ˣ⁄ₘ versus pressure p, at sufficiently high pressure, the extent of adsorption
options: becomes independent of pressure, reaching a saturation value as all available adsorption sites become occupied
continues to increase indefinitely and without limit as pressure increases further
suddenly and abruptly drops to zero regardless of the specific adsorbate-adsorbent system
increases in a perfectly linear (straight line) fashion at all pressures without exception
explanation: At sufficiently high pressures, the amount of gas adsorbed on a solid surface tends to approach a saturation value and becomes essentially independent of further pressure increases, since all the available adsorption sites on the finite solid surface have become occupied, a limiting behaviour that the empirical Freundlich isotherm approximates reasonably well at moderate pressures but does not perfectly capture at the very highest pressure extremes

subject: Chemistry
question: When a solid adsorbent like activated charcoal is used to decolorize a solution (removing colored impurities), this process demonstrates
options: adsorption occurring from the solution phase, with the colored impurity molecules being adsorbed onto the solid surface
absorption of the colored impurity uniformly throughout the bulk of the charcoal
a chemical reaction that permanently destroys the colored impurity molecules
the complete evaporation of the colored impurity from the solution
explanation: The decolorization of a solution using activated charcoal is a classic example of adsorption occurring from the solution phase, in which the colored impurity molecules present in the liquid solution become adsorbed onto the extensive surface area of the solid charcoal adsorbent, effectively removing the color from the solution

subject: Chemistry
question: According to the adsorption theory of heterogeneous catalysis, the reaction proceeds through several steps, beginning with
options: adsorption (diffusion) of the gaseous reactant molecules onto the surface of the solid catalyst
immediate desorption of the reactant molecules without any prior adsorption occurring
direct reaction of the reactants in the bulk gas phase, entirely independent of the solid catalyst surface
the solid catalyst dissolving completely into the reactant mixture
explanation: The adsorption theory of heterogeneous catalysis describes a multi-step mechanism that begins with the diffusion and adsorption of the gaseous reactant molecules onto the active sites present on the surface of the solid catalyst, which is followed by subsequent steps including the actual chemical reaction occurring between the adsorbed species, and finally desorption of the product molecules from the catalyst surface

subject: Chemistry
question: The activity of a solid catalyst is closely related to its ability to
options: chemisorb the reactant molecules with an appropriate (neither too strong nor too weak) strength of interaction
physisorb the reactant molecules as weakly as possible with minimal interaction
completely prevent any interaction whatsoever with the reactant molecules
react permanently and irreversibly with the reactant molecules, consuming the catalyst
explanation: The catalytic activity of a solid catalyst is strongly correlated with its ability to chemisorb reactant molecules with an appropriately intermediate strength of interaction, since chemisorption too weak fails to sufficiently activate the reactant molecules, while chemisorption too strong can prevent proper desorption of products, both scenarios limiting overall catalytic efficiency

subject: Chemistry
question: The selectivity of a catalyst refers to its ability to
options: direct a chemical reaction to yield one particular desired product preferentially, out of several thermodynamically possible products
increase the rate of every possible reaction pathway equally and without any preference
function effectively as a catalyst for absolutely any type of chemical reaction
remain completely inert and non-functional under all experimental conditions
explanation: Selectivity refers to the specific ability of a catalyst to direct a chemical reaction along a particular pathway, yielding one desired product preferentially over other possible products that might form from the same set of starting reactants under different (uncatalyzed or differently catalyzed) conditions

subject: Chemistry
question: Zeolites function as shape-selective catalysts because their microporous structure
options: restricts which reactant or product molecules can enter or exit the catalytic pores based on their molecular size and shape
allows literally any molecule of any size or shape to pass through completely unrestricted
has absolutely no defined pore structure of any kind whatsoever
functions purely through non-selective physisorption with no structural size restriction involved
explanation: Zeolites possess a highly regular, microporous crystalline framework with precisely defined pore and channel sizes, and this structural feature restricts which reactant molecules can access the internal catalytic active sites and which product molecules can subsequently exit the pore structure, based specifically on molecular size and shape, giving rise to their characteristic shape-selective catalytic behaviour

subject: Chemistry
question: The mechanism of enzyme catalysis is often described using the lock and key model, in which
options: the specific three dimensional shape of the enzyme's active site precisely complements the shape of the substrate molecule, similar to a key fitting into a specific lock
the enzyme has no specific structural requirement whatsoever and can bind to literally any substrate randomly
the substrate molecule permanently and irreversibly destroys the structure of the enzyme upon binding
enzymes function through an entirely different mechanism completely unrelated to any structural complementarity
explanation: The lock and key model of enzyme catalysis proposes that the specific three dimensional shape of an enzyme's active site is precisely complementary to the shape of its particular substrate molecule, much like a specific key fitting into its corresponding lock, explaining the high degree of substrate specificity characteristic of most enzymes

subject: Chemistry
question: Compared to typical inorganic catalysts, enzymes generally show significantly greater catalytic efficiency and specificity, but are also characterized by
options: being highly sensitive to conditions such as temperature and pH, often becoming denatured and losing activity outside a narrow optimal range
being completely insensitive to any changes in temperature or pH under all conditions
functioning equally well and with identical efficiency at any temperature, including extremely high temperatures
requiring no specific optimal conditions whatsoever to maintain their catalytic function
explanation: While enzymes typically offer dramatically greater catalytic efficiency and substrate specificity compared to conventional inorganic catalysts, they are also characteristically quite sensitive to environmental conditions such as temperature and pH, often undergoing denaturation (a loss of their specific three dimensional structure and hence catalytic function) if conditions deviate significantly outside their narrow optimal range

subject: Chemistry
topic: Classification of Colloids: Dispersion Medium Water
question: A colloidal system in which both the dispersed phase and dispersion medium are liquids, such as milk, is specifically classified as an
options: emulsion
aerosol
foam exclusively
gel exclusively
explanation: A colloidal system consisting of one liquid finely dispersed within another, immiscible liquid, such as the fat globules dispersed within the aqueous phase of milk, is specifically classified as an emulsion

subject: Chemistry
question: Dialysis, a method used to purify colloidal solutions, involves separating dissolved ionic impurities from colloidal particles using a
options: semipermeable membrane that allows small ions to pass through while retaining the larger colloidal particles
completely impermeable membrane that blocks the passage of both ions and colloidal particles equally
filter paper with pores far too small to allow even the smallest ions through
centrifuge operating at extremely low rotational speeds with no membrane involved
explanation: Dialysis is a purification technique for colloidal solutions that uses a semipermeable membrane, through which small dissolved ionic impurities can pass and be washed away, while the much larger colloidal particles are retained on the other side of the membrane, effectively purifying the colloidal solution

subject: Chemistry
question: Electrodialysis, an accelerated version of ordinary dialysis, speeds up the removal of ionic impurities from a colloidal solution by
options: applying an electric field across the semipermeable membrane, which increases the rate of migration of the charged ionic impurities
completely eliminating the need for any semipermeable membrane whatsoever
using an extremely high temperature to boil off all ionic impurities directly
adding additional colloidal particles to dilute the concentration of ionic impurities
explanation: Electrodialysis accelerates the standard dialysis process by applying an external electric field across the semipermeable membrane, which increases the migration rate of the charged ionic impurities toward the appropriately charged electrode, speeding up their removal from the colloidal solution compared to ordinary dialysis relying on simple diffusion alone

subject: Chemistry
question: According to the Hardy-Schulze rule, the coagulating power of an electrolyte ion used to precipitate a colloidal sol
options: increases with the increasing magnitude of charge on the ion that carries a charge opposite to that of the colloidal particles
depends only on the mass of the ion, with charge having absolutely no relevance whatsoever
is completely identical for all ions regardless of their charge or identity
depends exclusively on the color of the ion in question
explanation: The Hardy-Schulze rule states that the coagulating (precipitating) power of an electrolyte ion with a charge opposite to that of the colloidal particles increases significantly with the increasing magnitude (valency) of that ion's charge, meaning a trivalent ion is generally far more effective at coagulating an oppositely charged sol than a monovalent ion of similar concentration

subject: Chemistry
question: Lyophilic colloids can be used to protect lyophobic colloids from coagulation, and the numerical measure of this protective ability is called the
options: gold number
Hardy-Schulze value
Tyndall coefficient
electrophoretic mobility index
explanation: The gold number is a numerical value that measures the protective capacity of a lyophilic colloid, defined as the minimum mass (in milligrams) of the protective lyophilic colloid required to prevent the coagulation of a standard gold sol when a specified amount of an electrolyte (such as sodium chloride) is added, with a smaller gold number indicating a greater protective capacity

subject: Chemistry
question: Peptization is a method for preparing a colloidal sol from a freshly precipitated substance by
options: adding a small amount of a suitable electrolyte, causing the precipitate to disperse into colloidal sized particles
adding a large excess of a completely unrelated electrolyte to permanently dissolve the precipitate as a true solution
heating the precipitate to an extremely high temperature until it fully vaporizes
physically crushing the precipitate using extremely high mechanical pressure alone
explanation: Peptization is a chemical method for converting a freshly prepared precipitate into a colloidal sol by adding a small, appropriate amount of a suitable electrolyte, which becomes preferentially adsorbed onto the precipitate particles, imparting a common surface charge that causes the particles to disperse and repel one another, forming a stable colloidal suspension

subject: Chemistry
question: Colloidal solutions generally show much smaller colligative property effects (such as osmotic pressure) compared to true solutions of the same mass concentration mainly because
options: colloidal particles are considerably larger and hence far fewer in number (lower molar concentration) than the corresponding number of dissolved molecules or ions in an equivalent mass of true solution
colloidal particles have no measurable mass whatsoever, unlike molecules in a true solution
colligative properties depend exclusively on particle size rather than particle number in any solution type
colloidal solutions always exist at a much higher effective temperature than true solutions
explanation: Since colligative properties fundamentally depend on the number (molar concentration) of dispersed particles rather than their mass, and since colloidal particles are considerably larger (and hence present in much smaller numbers for a given total mass) compared to the individual molecules or ions present in an equivalent mass concentration of a true solution, colloidal solutions typically exhibit much smaller colligative property effects, such as lower osmotic pressure, for the same mass concentration of dispersed substance

subject: Chemistry
topic: Applications of Colloids: Alum in Water Purification
question: Alum is commonly added during municipal water purification processes primarily because it
options: coagulates and removes suspended colloidal impurities present in the raw water, clarifying it
acts as a disinfectant that directly kills harmful bacteria and pathogens
increases the dissolved oxygen content of the treated water significantly
chemically removes dissolved salts and minerals from the water
explanation: Alum, when added to raw water, dissociates to release aluminium ions that effectively coagulate the negatively charged colloidal clay and other suspended impurities naturally present in the water, causing them to aggregate and settle out, thereby clarifying and purifying the water before further treatment steps such as disinfection

subject: Chemistry
question: An emulsion consisting of oil droplets dispersed in water is called an
options: oil in water emulsion
water in oil emulsion
oil in oil emulsion
water in water emulsion
explanation: An emulsion in which small oil droplets are dispersed throughout a continuous water phase is specifically classified as an oil in water (O/W) emulsion, exemplified by milk

subject: Chemistry
question: Emulsifying agents (emulsifiers) such as soap help stabilize an emulsion by
options: forming a protective interfacial layer around the dispersed droplets, preventing them from coalescing back together
chemically reacting with and permanently destroying one of the two immiscible liquid phases
increasing the surface tension between the two immiscible liquids significantly
having absolutely no effect on the stability of the resulting emulsion whatsoever
explanation: An emulsifying agent, such as soap, functions by forming a thin protective interfacial film or layer around the small dispersed liquid droplets within an emulsion, reducing the interfacial tension between the two immiscible liquid phases and physically preventing the individual droplets from coalescing (merging) back together, thereby stabilizing the emulsion

subject: Chemistry
question: Micelles, formed by soap or detergent molecules in water above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), arrange with their
options: hydrophobic tails oriented towards the interior and hydrophilic heads oriented towards the exterior, facing the surrounding water
hydrophilic heads oriented towards the interior and hydrophobic tails facing the surrounding water
both hydrophobic and hydrophilic portions oriented randomly with no defined structural arrangement
entire molecular structure oriented in a single flat plane with no three dimensional arrangement
explanation: When surfactant molecules like soap aggregate to form micelles in water above the critical micelle concentration, they arrange themselves with their hydrophobic (water-repelling) hydrocarbon tails oriented towards the interior of the spherical micelle (away from water), while their hydrophilic (water-attracting) polar or ionic head groups remain oriented towards the exterior, in direct contact with the surrounding water molecules

subject: Chemistry
question: Colloidal gold sols can be prepared by Bredig's arc method, which involves
options: striking an electric arc between gold metal electrodes immersed in water, causing gold vapor to condense into colloidal sized particles
simply dissolving solid gold metal directly and completely in ordinary water
chemically reducing a gold salt using an extremely weak, ineffective reducing agent
heating solid gold metal to an extremely high temperature in the complete absence of any liquid medium
explanation: Bredig's arc method prepares colloidal metal sols, such as colloidal gold, by striking an electric arc between two metal electrodes (made of the desired metal) immersed in the dispersion medium (such as chilled water); the intense heat vaporizes some of the metal, which is then immediately condensed by the surrounding cold water into extremely fine colloidal sized particles

subject: Chemistry
question: Adsorption indicators, used in certain types of precipitation titrations, function by
options: changing color when they become selectively adsorbed onto the surface of the precipitate at the equivalence point of the titration
reacting chemically and irreversibly with the titrant before the equivalence point is reached
having absolutely no relationship whatsoever to any surface adsorption phenomenon despite their name
functioning identically in every respect to ordinary acid-base indicators with no distinguishing characteristics
explanation: Adsorption indicators are substances that become selectively adsorbed onto the surface of a precipitate specifically at or very near the equivalence point of certain precipitation titrations, and this adsorption event causes a distinct, visible color change in the indicator, signaling that the titration endpoint has been reached

subject: Chemistry
question: Ultrafiltration is a purification technique for colloidal solutions that uses
options: specially prepared filter paper with pores small enough to retain colloidal particles while allowing dissolved ions and small molecules to pass through
ordinary filter paper with pores far too large to retain even the largest colloidal particles
a semipermeable membrane exclusively with no filter paper involved at any stage
high speed centrifugation exclusively with no filtration step involved whatsoever
explanation: Ultrafiltration uses specially prepared filter paper (often impregnated with a suitable substance like collodion) with pore sizes small enough to retain the larger colloidal particles while allowing smaller dissolved ions and molecules to pass through, providing an alternative purification method to dialysis for separating colloidal particles from dissolved impurities

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Langmuir Adsorption Isotherm
question: The Langmuir adsorption isotherm, unlike the purely empirical Freundlich isotherm, is derived from a theoretical model that assumes
options: adsorption occurs as a monolayer on a surface with a fixed, finite number of equivalent adsorption sites, with no interaction between adjacent adsorbed molecules
adsorption can continue indefinitely to form an unlimited number of molecular layers on the surface without any restriction
every adsorption site on the surface has a completely different, unique energy of interaction with the adsorbate
the rate of adsorption is entirely independent of the pressure or concentration of the adsorbate at all times
explanation: The Langmuir adsorption isotherm is derived from a specific theoretical model that assumes adsorption occurs as a single monomolecular layer (monolayer) on a solid surface possessing a fixed, finite number of equivalent (energetically identical) adsorption sites, with the further assumption that there is no significant interaction between adjacent adsorbed molecules on neighbouring sites, providing a more theoretically grounded framework compared to the purely empirical Freundlich isotherm equation

subject: Chemistry
topic: Comparative Analysis: Adsorption versus Absorption Kinetics
question: Experimentally, adsorption can typically be distinguished from absorption by observing that
options: adsorption occurs rapidly at the surface and reaches a measurable equilibrium quickly, whereas absorption, requiring diffusion of the substance throughout the entire bulk material, generally proceeds at a comparatively much slower overall rate
absorption always occurs faster than adsorption under every conceivable set of experimental conditions
both processes occur at exactly identical rates in every case with no measurable difference whatsoever
neither adsorption nor absorption can ever be distinguished experimentally through any kinetic measurement
explanation:
Since adsorption is confined to the surface of a material, it typically reaches a measurable equilibrium state relatively quickly, as the process does not require extensive penetration into the bulk
Absorption, in contrast, requires the substance being absorbed to diffuse throughout the entire bulk volume of the absorbing material, a process that is generally rate-limited by diffusion and therefore proceeds at a considerably slower overall rate compared to the essentially surface-confined process of adsorption, providing one practical experimental means of distinguishing between the two phenomena

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Catalyst Poisoning Mechanism
question: Catalytic poisoning, such as the deactivation of a platinum catalyst by trace amounts of sulfur compounds, occurs mechanistically because the poison
options: becomes strongly and preferentially chemisorbed onto the active catalytic sites of the solid catalyst, blocking these sites from further interaction with the intended reactant molecules
reacts chemically with the reactant molecules directly, entirely independent of any interaction with the catalyst surface itself
increases the overall surface area of the catalyst, paradoxically decreasing its measured activity per unit area
exists only in the gas phase and never makes physical contact with the solid catalyst surface at any point
explanation: Catalytic poisons typically function mechanistically by becoming strongly and often essentially irreversibly chemisorbed onto the specific active sites present on a solid catalyst's surface, effectively occupying and blocking these sites so that the intended reactant molecules can no longer access them for the catalyzed reaction to proceed, which is precisely why even very small (trace) quantities of a strongly binding poison substance can dramatically and often permanently reduce or completely eliminate the effective catalytic activity of the affected catalyst

subject: Chemistry
topic: Multi-step Analysis of Heterogeneous Catalytic Mechanism
question: In the complete adsorption theory mechanism of heterogeneous catalysis, following the initial diffusion and adsorption of reactants onto the catalyst surface, the subsequent rate-determining step often involves
options: the actual chemical reaction occurring between the adsorbed reactant species while still bound to the catalyst surface, forming adsorbed product species
the immediate and instantaneous desorption of unreacted starting reactant molecules with no chemical transformation occurring at all
a completely separate, entirely independent reaction occurring simultaneously in the bulk gas phase, unrelated to the catalyst surface
the permanent and total consumption of the solid catalyst material itself during each individual catalytic cycle
explanation: Within the complete multi-step mechanism proposed by the adsorption theory of heterogeneous catalysis, after the initial diffusion and chemisorption of reactant molecules onto active sites of the catalyst surface, the subsequent step commonly identified as rate-determining involves the actual chemical transformation (reaction) occurring between the adsorbed reactant species while they remain bound to the catalyst surface, converting them into adsorbed product species, which must then subsequently desorb from the surface and diffuse away to complete the overall catalytic cycle

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Enzyme Kinetics: Michaelis-Menten Behaviour
question: In enzyme catalyzed reactions, the observed reaction rate typically increases with increasing substrate concentration at low concentrations, but eventually approaches a maximum, constant rate at very high substrate concentrations, a behaviour explained by the fact that
options: at sufficiently high substrate concentration, essentially all available enzyme active sites become saturated (fully occupied) with bound substrate, so further increasing substrate concentration cannot increase the rate any further
enzymes become completely and permanently destroyed at any substrate concentration exceeding a certain threshold value
the reaction spontaneously and completely reverses in direction once a specific substrate concentration is exceeded
substrate concentration has no relevance whatsoever to the observed rate of any enzyme catalyzed reaction
explanation: At low substrate concentrations, increasing the substrate concentration increases the reaction rate because more enzyme active sites become occupied by substrate molecules as availability increases; however, at sufficiently high substrate concentrations, essentially all of the finite number of available enzyme active sites become saturated (fully occupied) with bound substrate molecules, meaning the enzyme is working at its maximum possible capacity, and further increases in substrate concentration beyond this saturation point cannot increase the observed reaction rate any further, explaining the characteristic saturation kinetics (approaching a maximum rate, Vmax) observed for many enzyme-catalyzed reactions, as formally described by Michaelis-Menten kinetics

subject: Chemistry
topic: Thermodynamic Basis of Colloidal Stability: Zeta Potential
question: The electrokinetic (zeta) potential, associated with the electric double layer surrounding a charged colloidal particle, is significant for colloidal stability because
options: a sufficiently high zeta potential magnitude generates strong electrostatic repulsion between neighbouring colloidal particles, preventing them from approaching closely enough to aggregate and coagulate
zeta potential has absolutely no relationship whatsoever to the electrostatic repulsion between colloidal particles
a lower zeta potential magnitude always corresponds to greater colloidal stability in every case, with no exception
zeta potential exclusively determines the visible color of a colloidal solution with no bearing on its physical stability
explanation: The zeta potential represents the effective electric potential at the boundary of the electric double layer surrounding a charged colloidal particle, and when this zeta potential magnitude is sufficiently high, the resulting electrostatic repulsive forces between neighbouring, similarly charged colloidal particles are strong enough to prevent them from approaching closely enough for short range attractive van der Waals forces to dominate and cause aggregation, thereby maintaining the overall stability of the colloidal dispersion; conversely, reducing the magnitude of this zeta potential (such as through the addition of an appropriate electrolyte) diminishes this stabilizing repulsion and promotes coagulation

subject: Chemistry
topic: Comparative Analysis of Coagulating Power: Valency Effects
question: When comparing the relative coagulating power of Al³⁺, Ba²⁺, and Na⁺ ions for precipitating a negatively charged colloidal sol, the Hardy-Schulze rule predicts an order of
options: Al³⁺ much greater than Ba²⁺ much greater than Na⁺, corresponding directly to their increasing ionic charge (valency)
Na⁺ much greater than Ba²⁺ much greater than Al³⁺, in the reverse order of increasing charge
all three ions showing exactly identical coagulating power regardless of their differing charge
coagulating power being determined solely by ionic radius, with charge having no relevance whatsoever
explanation: According to the Hardy-Schulze rule, the coagulating power of an ion (of charge opposite to the colloidal particles) increases dramatically with increasing ionic charge (valency), so for a negatively charged colloidal sol, the trivalent Al³⁺ ion would be expected to show by far the greatest coagulating power, followed by the divalent Ba²⁺ ion, with the monovalent Na⁺ ion showing the weakest coagulating power among the three, consistent with the general observation that coagulating power increases sharply, often by several orders of magnitude, with each additional unit of ionic charge

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Lyophilic Colloid Stability Mechanisms
question: Lyophilic colloids owe their inherent stability primarily to a combination of
options: both the electrical charge on the dispersed particles and extensive solvation (hydration in aqueous systems) of the particle surface by the surrounding dispersion medium
exclusively the electrical charge on the particles, with solvation playing absolutely no role whatsoever
exclusively solvation of the particle surface, with electrical charge playing absolutely no role whatsoever
neither electrical charge nor solvation, but purely the small physical size of the dispersed particles alone
explanation: The characteristic high stability of lyophilic colloids arises from a combination of two contributing factors: the electrical charge typically present on the dispersed particles (providing electrostatic repulsion, similar to lyophobic sols), and additionally, extensive solvation of the particle surfaces by the surrounding dispersion medium (such as hydration in aqueous lyophilic sols), which creates a protective solvent shell around each particle that further hinders close approach and aggregation, together explaining why lyophilic colloids generally show substantially greater stability against coagulation compared to lyophobic colloids, which rely on charge stabilization alone

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Shape-Selective Catalysis Mechanism
question: In the shape-selective catalytic conversion of methanol to gasoline using the synthetic zeolite ZSM-5, the specific pore geometry of the zeolite framework functions to
options: restrict the reaction pathway such that only linear or moderately branched hydrocarbon products of a size compatible with the pore dimensions can be formed and subsequently diffuse out of the catalyst structure
allow the unrestricted formation of hydrocarbon products of literally any size or degree of branching without any structural limitation whatsoever
completely and permanently prevent any chemical reaction from occurring within the zeolite pore structure
function purely as an inert physical support material with no actual catalytic or shape-selective role whatsoever
explanation: In the shape-selective conversion of methanol to gasoline range hydrocarbons using ZSM-5 zeolite, the precisely defined pore and channel dimensions of the zeolite framework restrict the reaction such that only hydrocarbon product molecules of a size and shape compatible with the pore geometry can effectively form within, and subsequently diffuse out of, the catalytic pore structure, effectively excluding the formation of excessively large or highly branched hydrocarbon products that would be unable to fit through or navigate the constrained pore network, giving this catalytic process its valuable shape-selectivity for producing gasoline range products

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Emulsion Type Determination: Dye Test
question: The dye solubility test, used to experimentally determine whether an unknown emulsion is oil in water or water in oil type, works by adding a small amount of a water soluble dye and observing that
options: if the entire continuous phase of the emulsion becomes colored, the emulsion is of the oil in water type, since the dye readily dissolves throughout the continuous aqueous phase
the dye always colors only the dispersed phase regardless of the emulsion type, providing no useful diagnostic information whatsoever
water soluble dyes are entirely incapable of dissolving in either phase of any emulsion under any circumstances
the test result depends exclusively on the specific color of the dye chosen, with no relevance to the underlying emulsion type
explanation:
The dye solubility test exploits the fact that a small amount of an added water-soluble dye will readily dissolve throughout and color the entire continuous (bulk) phase of an emulsion if that continuous phase is aqueous (water), which occurs specifically in an oil in water emulsion
If instead only small, discrete colored droplets are observed dispersed throughout an uncolored bulk phase, this indicates that the continuous phase is actually oil (not water), corresponding to a water in oil type emulsion, providing a simple and effective experimental method for distinguishing between the two possible emulsion types

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Kinetic Analysis of Autocatalytic Reactions
question: A characteristic feature of autocatalytic reactions, distinguishing their kinetic behaviour from ordinary (non-autocatalytic) reactions, is that the reaction rate
options: initially increases over time as the autocatalytic product accumulates and its concentration builds up, before eventually decreasing again as the reactant becomes substantially depleted
continuously and monotonically decreases from the very beginning of the reaction, exactly like most ordinary, non-autocatalytic reactions
remains perfectly constant throughout the entire course of the reaction from start to finish, regardless of any changing concentrations
becomes completely and permanently zero from the very instant the reaction begins, with no measurable progress ever occurring
explanation: A distinguishing kinetic characteristic of autocatalytic reactions is that, because the reaction rate depends positively on the concentration of a product that is itself accumulating as the reaction proceeds, the observed reaction rate often initially increases over time (in contrast to the typically monotonically decreasing rate observed for most ordinary reactions as reactant concentration steadily depletes), reaching a maximum rate at some intermediate point, before eventually decreasing again as the original reactant becomes substantially consumed and depleted later in the reaction, producing a characteristic sigmoidal (S-shaped) concentration versus time profile rather than the simple decay curve typical of non-autocatalytic reactions

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Thermodynamic Analysis of Reversible Chemisorption
question: While chemisorption is generally considered irreversible under ordinary conditions due to the strength of the chemical bonds formed, certain chemisorption processes can become effectively reversible at sufficiently elevated temperatures because
options: the increased thermal energy at high temperature can become comparable to or exceed the activation energy required to break the chemical bonds holding the chemisorbed species to the surface, allowing desorption to occur
chemical bonds formed during chemisorption fundamentally become weaker in an absolute sense as temperature increases, contradicting the general principles of chemical bonding
reversibility in chemisorption has no meaningful relationship whatsoever to temperature under any circumstances
chemisorbed species spontaneously transform into an entirely different, unrelated chemical substance once a specific temperature threshold is exceeded
explanation:
Although chemisorption is generally treated as an essentially irreversible process under typical, moderate experimental conditions due to the considerable strength of the chemical bonds formed between adsorbate and adsorbent, at sufficiently elevated temperatures, the thermal energy available to the system can become large enough to overcome the activation energy barrier associated with breaking these chemical bonds, allowing the chemisorbed species to be desorbed from the surface
This temperature-dependent reversibility, while requiring considerably more thermal energy input than would be needed to reverse comparatively weak physisorption interactions, demonstrates that the practical irreversibility commonly associated with chemisorption is fundamentally a kinetic limitation related to a high activation energy barrier for desorption, rather than an absolute thermodynamic impossibility of reversal under any conditions whatsoever

subject: Chemistry
topic: Comparative Analysis of Homogeneous versus Heterogeneous Catalysis Recovery
question: One notable industrial advantage of heterogeneous catalysis over homogeneous catalysis is that heterogeneous catalysts, existing in a distinct physical phase from the reaction mixture, can typically be
options: more easily and simply separated and recovered from the final product mixture through straightforward physical means such as filtration, allowing convenient catalyst reuse
only ever separated from the reaction mixture through complex, expensive chemical reactions that consume the catalyst entirely
never successfully recovered or reused under any practical industrial circumstances whatsoever
identical in every practical respect to homogeneous catalysts regarding ease of separation and recovery
explanation:
Since a heterogeneous catalyst exists in a physically distinct phase (most commonly solid) compared to the surrounding liquid or gaseous reaction mixture, it can typically be separated and recovered from the final product mixture through comparatively simple and cost-effective physical separation methods, such as filtration or centrifugation, allowing the recovered catalyst to be conveniently reused in subsequent reaction batches
This practical advantage of straightforward catalyst recovery and reuse is a significant reason why heterogeneous catalysis is often industrially preferred over homogeneous catalysis, where the catalyst exists dissolved within the same phase as the reactants and products, generally requiring more complex and costly separation procedures such as distillation or specialized extraction techniques to recover and reuse the catalyst

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Protective Colloid Action Mechanism
question: When a lyophilic colloid such as gelatin is added to protect a lyophobic gold sol from electrolyte-induced coagulation, the protective mechanism operates by
options: the lyophilic colloid molecules adsorbing onto and forming a protective coating around the individual lyophobic (gold) particles, effectively imparting the greater inherent stability characteristics of the lyophilic colloid to the otherwise less stable lyophobic particles
the lyophilic colloid chemically reacting with and completely converting all the lyophobic gold particles into an entirely different, unrelated chemical compound
the lyophilic colloid simply increasing the overall temperature of the mixed colloidal system to a level that prevents any possible coagulation from occurring
the lyophilic colloid having absolutely no meaningful physical or chemical interaction whatsoever with the lyophobic particles present in the mixed system
explanation:
The protective action of a lyophilic colloid, such as gelatin, added to stabilize an otherwise more easily coagulated lyophobic sol like colloidal gold, operates through the lyophilic colloid molecules becoming adsorbed onto the surface of each individual lyophobic particle, effectively forming a protective coating layer around them
This adsorbed lyophilic coating imparts some of the greater inherent stability characteristics (including enhanced solvation and steric stabilization) of the lyophilic colloid to the coated lyophobic particles, making the overall protected colloidal system considerably more resistant to coagulation upon subsequent addition of an electrolyte, compared to the unprotected lyophobic sol alone

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Freundlich Isotherm Linearization
question: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm equation, ˣ⁄ₘ=k p^(¹⁄ₙ), can be conveniently linearized for graphical analysis by taking the logarithm of both sides, yielding the linear equation
options: log(ˣ⁄ₘ) = log k + (¹⁄ₙ) log p, allowing k and n to be determined from the intercept and slope respectively of a plot of log(ˣ⁄ₘ) versus log p
ˣ⁄ₘ = k+ (¹⁄ₙ)p directly, with no logarithmic transformation required at all
log(ˣ⁄ₘ) = k × log(¹⁄ₙ) × log p, combining all three quantities multiplicatively
p = k(ˣ⁄ₘ) raised to the power n, representing an entirely different, unrelated equation altogether
explanation: Taking the logarithm of both sides of the Freundlich isotherm equation ˣ⁄ₘ=k p^(¹⁄ₙ) yields the linear form log(ˣ⁄ₘ)=log k + (¹⁄ₙ) log p, which shows that a plot of log(ˣ⁄ₘ) on the y-axis against log p on the x-axis should produce a straight line, with the y-intercept of this line equal to log k (allowing k to be calculated) and the slope of the line equal to ¹⁄ₙ (allowing n to be calculated), providing a standard, convenient graphical method for experimentally determining the two empirical Freundlich constants from adsorption data collected at a series of different equilibrium pressures

subject: Chemistry
topic: Colloidal Particle Size and Surface Area Relationship
question: As a given mass of a solid substance is progressively subdivided into smaller and smaller colloidal sized particles, the total surface area of the substance
options: increases dramatically, since surface area increases as particle size decreases for a fixed total volume or mass of material
decreases significantly, since smaller particles inherently possess less total surface area than larger particles of the same total mass
remains completely unchanged regardless of how finely the substance is subdivided into smaller particles
becomes entirely undefined and impossible to calculate once particles reach colloidal dimensions
explanation: For a fixed total mass or volume of a solid substance, progressively subdividing it into a greater number of smaller individual particles dramatically increases the total surface area, since surface area scales with the square of a characteristic particle dimension while volume (and hence the number of particles for fixed total mass) scales with the cube of that dimension, meaning many small particles collectively possess far more total surface area than one large particle of equivalent total mass, which is precisely why colloidal systems, with their extremely small particle sizes, exhibit dramatically enhanced surface-related phenomena such as adsorption

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Sol Formation Thermodynamics
question: The general reluctance of lyophobic sols to form spontaneously (unlike lyophilic sols, which form readily) is best explained thermodynamically by recognizing that
options: lyophobic sol formation typically involves a significant increase in interfacial (surface) free energy due to the large surface area created without a correspondingly favorable, strong interaction between the dispersed phase and dispersion medium to compensate for this energy cost
lyophobic sols always have a lower total energy state than the corresponding bulk material, making their formation always thermodynamically favorable and spontaneous
surface free energy considerations are entirely irrelevant to any aspect of colloidal sol formation or stability
lyophilic and lyophobic sols form through fundamentally identical thermodynamic pathways with no meaningful distinction between them
explanation:
The formation of any colloidal sol from a bulk substance necessarily involves creating a very large total surface area, which is generally associated with a significant increase in interfacial (surface) free energy compared to the original bulk material
For lyophilic sols, this energetically unfavorable increase in surface free energy is substantially offset (and often overcome) by strong, favorable solvation interactions between the dispersed phase and dispersion medium, allowing spontaneous sol formation; for lyophobic sols, lacking this strong compensating solvation interaction, the unfavorable surface free energy increase generally prevents spontaneous formation, which is why lyophobic sols typically require special preparation methods (such as chemical reduction, Bredig's arc method, or peptization) rather than forming on their own simply by mixing the dispersed phase with the dispersion medium

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Industrial Catalyst Design Trade-offs
question: In designing an industrial heterogeneous catalyst, engineers must often balance competing considerations of catalytic activity and selectivity, since a catalyst optimized purely for maximum activity might
options: also catalyze unwanted side reactions leading to a mixture of products, whereas a catalyst optimized specifically for high selectivity toward one desired product might sacrifice some overall reaction rate
always simultaneously achieve both perfect activity and perfect selectivity with no meaningful trade-off ever existing between these two properties
have absolutely no relationship whatsoever between its activity and its selectivity for any given industrial process
become completely inactive and non-functional the moment any selectivity consideration is taken into account during its design
explanation: Industrial catalyst design frequently involves navigating a genuine trade-off between maximizing catalytic activity (the overall rate of the desired reaction) and maximizing selectivity (the preferential formation of one specific desired product over other possible products), since a highly active catalyst capable of rapidly accelerating a wide range of reaction pathways might inadvertently also catalyze unwanted side reactions, producing an impure mixture of products and requiring additional costly separation steps, whereas a more selective catalyst, carefully designed to favor only the desired reaction pathway, might achieve excellent product purity but potentially at the cost of a somewhat lower overall reaction rate compared to a less selective, more broadly active alternative catalyst

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Analysis of Gold Number Interpretation
question: When comparing two different lyophilic protective colloids, one having a gold number of 0.5 and the other having a gold number of 25, the colloid with the gold number of 0.5 demonstrates
options: considerably greater protective power, since a smaller gold number indicates that a smaller mass of the protective colloid is needed to prevent coagulation of the standard gold sol
considerably weaker protective power, since gold number is directly (not inversely) proportional to protective capacity
exactly identical protective power to the colloid with gold number 25, since gold number bears no relationship whatsoever to protective capacity
protective power that cannot be determined or compared in any way from the given gold number values alone
explanation: Since the gold number is defined as the minimum mass of a protective lyophilic colloid required to just prevent coagulation of a standard gold sol under specified conditions, a smaller gold number value indicates that only a small amount of the protective colloid is needed to achieve this protective effect, corresponding to a greater (more efficient) protective capacity, while conversely, a larger gold number value (such as 25 compared to 0.5) indicates that a considerably larger amount of that colloid is required to achieve the same protective effect, corresponding to a comparatively weaker protective capacity for that particular lyophilic colloid

subject: Chemistry
topic: Advanced Mechanistic Comparison of Physisorption Multilayers
question: Unlike chemisorption, which is generally restricted to forming only a single monomolecular layer on the adsorbent surface, physisorption can sometimes result in the formation of
options: multiple superimposed layers of adsorbate molecules (multilayer adsorption), since the weaker van der Waals forces responsible for physisorption can also act between already adsorbed molecules and additional incoming gas molecules
only a single monomolecular layer under all circumstances, with absolutely no possibility of any additional layers forming beyond the first
no adsorbed layer whatsoever under any experimental conditions, contradicting the fundamental definition of physisorption itself
exclusively three dimensional bulk crystalline structures rather than any planar or layered adsorbed structure of any kind
explanation:
Because chemisorption requires the formation of actual chemical bonds directly between adsorbate molecules and specific reactive sites on the underlying adsorbent surface, it is inherently limited to forming only a single monomolecular layer directly in contact with that surface
Physisorption, however, relying on comparatively weaker and less specific van der Waals forces, can in some cases result in the formation of multiple superimposed layers of adsorbate molecules (multilayer adsorption), since these weak attractive forces can also act between molecules within an already adsorbed first layer and additional incoming gas molecules from the surrounding gas phase, allowing subsequent layers to form on top of the initial physisorbed layer under suitable conditions of sufficiently high pressure and low temperature
